This vignette covers covariates (fixed effects) and random effects of the parameters of the growth curves, and likelihood ratio tests of their inclusion, for a height-diameter model of Scots pine trees and for counts of pods of faba bean plants. The growth models and their parameters are introduced in the vignette *Growth models and their parameters*.

## The pine data

The data set `PineHeightDiameter` contains the heights (m) and the diameters at breast height (cm) of 1678 Scots pine trees on 56 sample plots in eastern Finland, with the mean diameter `dmean` of the trees of each plot (Pukkala, 1989; Mehtätalo and Lappi, 2020). The explanatory variable is the diameter, not time: the height grows with the diameter towards an asymptote, from the breast height of 1.3 m at which the diameter is measured. The Chapman-Richards curve with the intercept $b_4 = 1.3$ fixed describes this (model M8 of Ciceu et al., 2020):

$$ h = 1.3 + b_1 \left(1 - \exp\left(-\frac{d}{b_3}\right)\right)^{\exp(b_2/b_3)}, $$

with the asymptote $b_1$ above breast height, the diameter $b_2$ at which the height grows fastest, and the scale $b_3$.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)
fit <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, data = PineHeightDiameter, model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
summary(fit)
ggplot(PineHeightDiameter, aes(x = dbh, y = height, colour = dmean)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(end = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", y = "Height (m)", colour = "Mean diameter\nof the plot (cm)",
       title = "1678 Scots pines on 56 plots") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Covariates and random effects

Covariates on the parameters are given by `fform`, e.g. `b1 ~ dmean` for an asymptote that depends on the mean diameter of the plot: trees of the same diameter are taller in plots of larger trees, a generalised height-diameter model. Random effects are given by `rform`, e.g. `b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot` for correlated random effects of each plot on the asymptote and on the diameter of the fastest growth in height, which account for the trees of a plot sharing their site and stand.

```{r}
fitdm <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, fform = b1 ~ dmean, data = PineHeightDiameter, model = "chapmanrichards",
               start = c(b4 = 1.3))
fitre <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, fform = b1 ~ dmean, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot, data = PineHeightDiameter,
               model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
summary(fitre)
```

### Testing the fixed effects

Likelihood ratio tests by `anova()` compare nested models, here with and without the effect of the mean diameter.

```{r}
fitre0 <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot, data = PineHeightDiameter, model = "chapmanrichards",
                start = c(b4 = 1.3))
anova(fitre0, fitre)
```

For gaussian (and lognormal) models without random effects, `test = "F"` gives F-tests as for `nls()`: the reduction of the residual sum of squares per additional parameter, divided by the residual mean square of the larger model. The F-test accounts for the estimation of the residual variance, which the likelihood ratio test does not, and is preferable for small data sets; here for the models without random effects:

```{r}
anova(fit, fitdm, test = "F")
```

The model without random effects treats the 1678 trees as independent, while the trees of a plot are alike, so its tests are too optimistic; the test with the random effects is the one to use.

### Testing the random effects

The random effects are tested in the same way, by likelihood ratio tests of the models with and without them: here without random effects, with a random asymptote, and with random asymptotes and diameters of the fastest growth.

```{r}
fitre1 <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, fform = b1 ~ dmean, rform = b1 ~ 1 | plot, data = PineHeightDiameter,
                model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
anova(fitdm, fitre1, fitre)
```

Under the smaller model, a standard deviation of the random effects is zero, on the boundary of its range, so the chi-square distribution of the likelihood ratio statistic is conservative: for a single standard deviation, the p-value is about twice the correct one. Both random effects are needed here anyway. `test = "boot"` gives a parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test, which simulates from the smaller model and does not rely on the chi-square distribution; it fits both models to each simulation and takes several minutes:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
anova(fitre1, fitre, test = "boot", nsim = 100, seed = 1)
```

The random effects of `b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot` are correlated. With a double bar, `b1 + b2 ~ 1 || plot`, they are independent, the same as `list(b1 ~ 1 | plot, b2 ~ 1 | plot)` and as `random = pdDiag(b1 + b2 ~ 1)` in nlme. A list of formulas mixes the two: `list(b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot, b3 ~ 1 | plot)` gives correlated random effects of $b_1$ and $b_2$, and a random effect of $b_3$ that is independent of both, a block-diagonal covariance matrix as `pdBlocked` in nlme. The likelihood ratio test of the correlated and the independent random effects tests their correlation:

```{r}
fitred <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, fform = b1 ~ dmean, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 || plot, data = PineHeightDiameter,
                model = "chapmanrichards", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
anova(fitred, fitre)
VarCorr(fitre)
```

The Wykoff curve, model M9 of Ciceu et al. (2020), with the same fixed and random effects, is an alternative height-diameter model; the models are not nested, and are compared by their AIC:

```{r}
fitwy <- gcTMB(height ~ dbh, fform = b1 ~ dmean, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plot, data = PineHeightDiameter,
               model = "wykoff", start = c(b4 = 1.3))
AIC(fitre, fitwy)
```

### Plotting the curves

`plot()` with `type = "curves"` draws a plot directly: the data with the curve of each plot, and the population curve as a thick line. By default the curves are drawn over the observed diameters; `times` gives the values at which they are drawn, here from a diameter of zero, where the curves start at breast height. It returns the ggplot object in a list, for changing the graph. A single numeric covariate such as `dmean` is shown on a continuous colour scale, with the population curves at three of its values. Otherwise, the plot can be constructed manually using `predict()`; for the population curves of plots with small, medium and large trees:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
p <- plot(fitre, type = "curves", times = seq(0, 52, by = 0.2), draw = FALSE)
p$curves + labs(x = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", y = "Height (m)", colour = "Mean diameter\nof the plot (cm)",
                title = "Curve of each plot (thin) and population curves (thick)",
                subtitle = "Population curves at the 10%, 50% and 90% quantiles of the mean diameter")
nd <- expand.grid(dbh = seq(0, 52, by = 0.2), dmean = c(10, 20, 30))
nd <- cbind(nd, predict(fitre, newdata = nd, random = FALSE, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(PineHeightDiameter, aes(x = dbh, y = height)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey80", size = 0.6) +
  geom_ribbon(data = nd, aes(x = dbh, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr, group = dmean, fill = dmean), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(data = nd, aes(y = fit, group = dmean, colour = dmean), linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(end = 0.9, breaks = c(10, 20, 30), aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  labs(x = "Diameter at breast height (cm)", y = "Height (m)", colour = "Mean diameter\nof the plot (cm)",
       fill = "Mean diameter\nof the plot (cm)", title = "Population curves with 95% confidence intervals",
       subtitle = "Trees of the same diameter are taller in plots of larger trees") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Non-normal responses

The `family` argument gives the distribution of the response: "gaussian", "lognormal", "poisson", "nbinom2", "nbinom1", "binomial", "betabinomial" or "beta". The data set `FabaCounts23` contains the numbers of pods of 22 faba bean plants of six genotypes, counted between 61 and 79 days after sowing. The plants have no pods at the first counts, so the threshold $b_4$, the time of the first pods, is identified by the zero counts and estimated; the asymmetry is fixed at $b_5 = 1$. A Poisson model with an asymptote and a time of the maximum growth rate for each genotype, and a random asymptote for each plant:

```{r}
fitp <- gcTMB(pods ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Genotype, rform = b1 ~ 1 | Tube_ID, data = FabaCounts23,
              family = "poisson", fix = c(b4 = FALSE))
summary(fitp)
genotypes <- data.frame(Genotype = sort(unique(FabaCounts23$Genotype)))
cbind(genotypes, predict(fitp, newdata = genotypes, type = "parameters", random = FALSE))
```

All the counts with the fitted curve of each plant, with its predicted random asymptote:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
days <- seq(61, 79, by = 0.05)
ndp <- merge(unique(FabaCounts23[, c("Tube_ID", "Genotype")]), data.frame(DAS = days))
ndp$fit <- predict(fitp, newdata = ndp)
ggplot(FabaCounts23, aes(x = DAS, y = pods, colour = Genotype)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(data = ndp, aes(y = fit, group = Tube_ID)) +
  labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Number of pods", colour = "Genotype") +
  theme_minimal()
```

By genotype, the curves of the plants together with the population curves of the genotypes (`random = FALSE`), the fixed effects, with 95% confidence intervals. For Poisson models, the confidence intervals of the mean are computed on the log scale, so that they stay positive.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
# the population curve of each genotype
ndg <- merge(genotypes, data.frame(DAS = days))
ndg <- cbind(ndg, predict(fitp, newdata = ndg, random = FALSE, interval = "confidence"))
ggplot(FabaCounts23, aes(x = DAS, y = pods)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ndg, aes(x = DAS, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "blue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(data = ndp, aes(y = fit, group = Tube_ID), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = ndg, aes(y = fit), colour = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Genotype) +
  labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Number of pods") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The estimated threshold improves the fit over the default threshold at sowing:

```{r}
fitp0 <- gcTMB(pods ~ DAS, fform = b1 + b2 ~ Genotype, rform = b1 ~ 1 | Tube_ID, data = FabaCounts23,
               family = "poisson")
AIC(fitp0, fitp)
```

### Checking a count model

For count data the Pearson residuals are not normal, even for a correct model. `plot()` therefore uses randomised quantile residuals by default (Dunn and Smyth, 1996). Each residual is the fitted distribution function at the observation, $F(y)$, mapped to the normal scale with $\Phi^{-1}$. For counts, $F$ jumps at each integer, so a value is drawn uniformly between $F(y - 1)$ and $F(y)$. Under the model the residuals are standard normal, so the QQ plot is compared with the identity line. The draws are random, and `seed` makes the plots reproducible.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
plot(fitp, seed = 1)
```

The simulations of `simulate()` can also be used for simulation-based residuals, for example with the package DHARMa (Hartig, 2026) and its function `createDHARMa()`. With `random = FALSE`, the simulations are conditional on the predicted random effects, like the residuals of `plot()`, and the simulation-based residuals are then essentially the same as the quantile residuals. With `random = TRUE`, new random effects are drawn for each simulation. Note that `random` means the opposite in `fitted()` and `residuals()`, where `random = TRUE` includes the predicted random effects.

Dunn, P.K. and Smyth, G.K. (1996). Randomized quantile residuals. *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics* 5, 236--244. doi:10.1080/10618600.1996.10474708.

Hartig, F. (2026). *DHARMa: Residual Diagnostics for Hierarchical (Multi-Level / Mixed) Regression Models*. R package version 0.5.1, doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.DHARMa.

Mehtätalo, L. and Lappi, J. (2020). *Biometry for Forestry and Environmental Data: with Examples in R*. Chapman and Hall/CRC, New York.

Pukkala, T. (1989). Prediction of tree diameter and height in a Scots pine stand as a function of the spatial pattern of trees. *Silva Fennica* 23, 83--99. doi:10.14214/sf.a15532.
